problemText: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land that connects two larger areas of land. Which of the four American regions is an isthmus?
choices: North America
South America
The Caribbean
Central America
hints: The isthmus joins the two continents together.
It sits between North America and South America.

problemText: A geography student is looking at a map and sees the Equator marked as a line running around the middle of Earth. She wants to identify which of the four American regions has land on both sides of the Equator. Based on where each region lies, which one should she identify?
choices: South America
Central America
North America
The Caribbean
hints: Three of the four regions lie entirely north of the Equator.
Only one region stretches far enough south for the Equator to cross through it.

problemText: A teacher asks her students to name a region that is not made up of one connected mainland but instead consists of many islands. Which of the four American regions fits this description?
choices: North America
The Caribbean
Central America
South America
hints: This region lies in and around a named sea, not connected as a single landmass.
The other three regions are either continents or a strip of land joining continents.

problemText: A traveler plans to walk from the northernmost part of North America all the way to the southernmost part of South America, staying on connected land the entire way and never stepping onto an island. She will cross through multiple regions in order from north to south. Which statement correctly lists the regions she will travel through and explains why one major region is left off the list?
choices: She travels through North America, the Caribbean, Central America, and South America, because the Caribbean Sea connects all four regions with landfills and bridges.
She travels through North America and South America only, because Central America is too narrow and mountainous for any person to cross safely on foot.
She travels through North America, Central America, and South America, because the Caribbean is a region of islands and she cannot reach it without crossing open ocean.
She travels through North America, Central America, the Caribbean, and South America in that order, because they form a continuous chain of connected landmasses from north to south.
hints: The Caribbean is made of islands, not connected mainland, so a land-only traveler cannot reach it.
Central America is the only landmass directly between the two continents.

problemText: A student makes two claims: (1) 'Central America is one of Earth's seven continents,' and (2) 'The Caribbean has land in both hemispheres because it lies near South America.' How many of these claims are correct, and why?
choices: Both claims are correct; Central America is a continent and the Caribbean extends across the Equator into the Southern Hemisphere.
Only the first claim is correct; Central America is indeed a continent, but the Caribbean lies entirely in the Northern Hemisphere since it does not cross the Equator.
Only the second claim is correct; the Caribbean does extend into both hemispheres, but Central America is not a continent but rather a bridge connecting the two continental landmasses.
Neither claim is correct; Central America is an isthmus joining two continents rather than a continent itself, and the Caribbean lies entirely north of the Equator.
hints: Two of Earth's seven continents are named in this topic; Central America is not one of them.
Being near South America does not automatically mean a region crosses the Equator.

problemText: A geographer draws a north-south line on a map and labels four regions along it in order: Region 1 at the top, Region 2 below it, Region 3 below Region 2, and Region 4 at the bottom. She states that Region 2 is a strip of land connecting two continents, Region 3 is made of islands and does not touch this north-south line, Region 4 has land in both hemispheres, and Region 1 is entirely north of the Equator. Which assignment of the four American regions to these positions is correct?
choices: Region 1 = North America, Region 2 = Central America, Region 3 = the Caribbean, Region 4 = South America
Region 1 = North America, Region 2 = the Caribbean, Region 3 = Central America, Region 4 = South America
Region 1 = Central America, Region 2 = North America, Region 3 = the Caribbean, Region 4 = South America
Region 1 = the Caribbean, Region 2 = Central America, Region 3 = North America, Region 4 = South America
hints: Central America is the isthmus that sits directly between the two continents on a north-south path, so it must be the strip of land described.
The Caribbean is islands lying off to the side, not on a straight north-south line through the connected landmasses.

problemText: A geographer creates a group name for several neighboring countries that share the same language family. What is this named group of countries called?
choices: A government
A continent
A region
A country
hints: The answer is the term for a named group of neighboring countries that share something in common.
This word is smaller than a continent but larger than a single country.

problemText: Three neighboring countries all border the same large ocean and export fish and seafood as major products. A mapmaker decides to group these three countries together under one region name because of what they have in common. What is the shared trait the mapmaker used to create this region?
choices: They all have coastlines that face mountains on their western side and plains on their eastern side
They each have a population of between 5 and 10 million people and similar government structures
They share a common language and celebrate the same national holidays each year
They border the same ocean and depend on ocean trade for exports
hints: Look for the trait mentioned in the problem that connects all three countries.
The reason a region is created is based on what the countries have in common, not just that they happen to be next to each other.

problemText: A student learns that South America is a continent made up of many countries. The student then hears about a region called Latin America, which also includes countries from Central America and the Caribbean. The student is confused because Latin America does not match the borders of South America exactly. Why might a region's border be drawn differently from a continent's border?
choices: A region's border is a choice made for a specific reason, while a continent's border follows the coastline of the land itself
Continents are created by government officials, while regions are created by individual mapmakers working alone
A region includes only countries that are independent nations, while a continent includes territories and islands that belong to other countries
The continent border is based on economic ties between neighboring countries, while the region border is based on physical size
hints: Think about what a continent's border is based on compared to what a region's border is based on.
A region's border comes from a choice someone made, not from a physical fact like a coast.

problemText: Two different geographers study the same group of five countries. Geographer A groups them into a region called the 'Highland Trade Zone' because the countries share mountain passes used for historical trade routes. Geographer B groups the same five countries into a region called the 'Monsoon Belt' because they all experience the same seasonal rain pattern. The two groupings include different borders and have different names. A student concludes that one geographer must be wrong. Why is the student's conclusion incorrect?
choices: Geographer A must be wrong because trade routes are used for commerce while climate patterns are studied by meteorologists, so they measure completely different things
Both geographers can be correct because each one grouped the countries by a different shared trait for a different reason
Geographer B must be wrong because seasonal rain patterns only affect agriculture, not the actual borders or identity of countries in a region
Both geographers are wrong because regions based on trade cannot overlap with regions based on climate in any location
hints: Remember that a region's border is a convention chosen by the person doing the grouping.
Consider whether two different sources can use two different shared traits and still both be valid.

problemText: A travel company creates region names to help tourists plan vacations. They group countries by which international airport hub most visitors fly into. At the same time, a wildlife conservation group creates different region names by grouping countries that share the same ecosystem and animal migration patterns. A country called Delphinia appears in the 'Eastern Hub Network' region on the travel company's map but appears in the 'Central Savanna' region on the conservation group's map. What does this tell you about how Delphinia can belong to more than one region?
choices: Delphinia must actually be two different countries with the same name, one located near the Eastern Hub Network and one located in the Central Savanna
Delphinia does not truly belong to any region because it is impossible for a single country to be classified by both transportation patterns and ecosystem types simultaneously
The travel company and conservation group are using different shared traits to group countries, so the same country can fit into different regions depending on the purpose
One of the two groups made an error and included Delphinia by mistake because each country can only appear in one region on one map
hints: Think about why each organization is grouping countries — what shared trait matters to each one?
A single country can belong to multiple regions if different sources are grouping by different traits.

problemText: A student reads two textbooks about world regions. Textbook 1 uses the region 'Southeast Asia' to mean nine specific countries grouped by geography and proximity to the same ocean. Textbook 2 uses 'Southeast Asia' to mean a different set of eight countries, grouped instead by historical trade partnerships and cultural connections along ancient merchant routes. The student asks: 'If Southeast Asia can have nine countries in one book and eight countries in another book, how do students ever agree on which countries are in a region?' What is the best answer to the student's question?
choices: Students cannot agree, which is why regions are not used by geographers anymore and modern geography relies only on latitude and longitude coordinates
There must be a single official list of countries in each region that both textbooks should have used correctly, established by an international geography authority
One textbook is for elementary students and is allowed to be wrong, while the other textbook is for high school and must be correct because older students learn the true boundaries
Students recognize that regions are named groups created for a purpose, so the same region name can include different countries depending on what shared trait a source chose to emphasize
hints: Remember that a region is a tool people create to organize a complicated world, not a fixed fact set by nature.
Different sources can have different reasons for grouping countries, and both can be useful even if they draw different borders around the same region name.

problemText: Which of these three regions sits directly on the northern shore of the Mediterranean Sea?
choices: Europe
Sub-Saharan Africa
The Middle East
The Sahara
hints: Use Question 1 of the routine: which region touches the Mediterranean's shore?
The Mediterranean has Europe along its northern edge and the African continent along its southern edge.

problemText: A traveler is standing on the northern shore of the Mediterranean Sea in the region of Europe. If she sails directly south across the sea to the African continent, which region will she reach?
choices: Sub-Saharan Africa, because Africa is directly south
The northern part of Africa, not Sub-Saharan Africa, because Sub-Saharan Africa lies far to the south beyond the Sahara
The Middle East, because it extends down the eastern coast of Africa and connects to the northern shore
The Sahara Desert region, because it is located on the African continent north of where Sub-Saharan Africa begins
hints: Remember that Sub-Saharan Africa is the region south of the Sahara, not the whole African continent.
What lies between the Mediterranean coast and Sub-Saharan Africa?

problemText: From a location in the Middle East at the eastern end of the Mediterranean Sea, in which direction would you need to travel to reach Europe on the northern shore of that same sea?
choices: South
North
West
East
hints: Use Question 2 of the routine: what direction takes you from one region to another?
Europe is on the northern shore and the Middle East is at the eastern end of the Mediterranean—which direction connects them?

problemText: A student claims: 'The Middle East must be in Africa, because it connects to the African continent by a narrow strip of land, just like Europe connects to Africa across the narrow water gap.' Identify the error in this claim and explain why the two connections are different.
choices: The error is that the Middle East is not connected to Africa at all; Europe is the only region that touches Africa.
The error is that the Middle East is actually in Europe, not near Africa, so the connection described does not exist.
The error is that there is no water gap between Europe and Africa; they are also connected by land like the Middle East is.

The error is that Europe and Africa are separated by water only, while the Middle East and the northeastern corner of Africa are joined by a narrow strip of land, so they are different types of connections.
hints: Think about Question 1 of the routine for each region: how do they sit relative to the Mediterranean Sea?
One connection is water-only, and one connection is by land—how does that difference matter for the regions?

problemText: If you start in Sub-Saharan Africa and travel north, which regions would you pass through before you reach the Mediterranean Sea? Explain which regions sit between Sub-Saharan Africa and the sea.
choices: You would pass through the northern part of the African continent (north of the Sahara), because the rest of Africa lies between Sub-Saharan Africa and the Mediterranean coast.
You would pass through the Sahara Desert and then the northern African coast, since these lie between Sub-Saharan Africa and the Mediterranean Sea
You would reach the Mediterranean directly without passing through any other region, because Sub-Saharan Africa extends all the way to the northern coast of the continent
You would pass through the Middle East first and then Europe, because both of these regions are positioned north of all parts of the African continent
hints: Sub-Saharan Africa is defined by being south of the Sahara—what is between the Sahara and the Mediterranean Sea?
Remember that Sub-Saharan Africa does not touch the Mediterranean Sea at all.

problemText: Two different mapmakers are making geography reference books. Mapmaker A groups Egypt with Sub-Saharan Africa because Egypt is on the African continent. Mapmaker B groups Egypt with the Middle East instead. Which mapmaker's choice can be defended, and why? What does this disagreement reveal about how regions are defined?
choices: Only Mapmaker A is correct, because Egypt is physically located on the African continent and physical location is the only rule that should determine regional grouping

Both mapmakers' choices can be defended, because Egypt sits north of the Sahara in the northeastern corner of Africa, and a region's border is chosen by whoever is doing the grouping rather than fixed by nature.
Only Mapmaker B is correct, because the Middle East is the only region that Egypt can belong to according to every authoritative geography source and standard map
Neither mapmaker is correct, because Egypt is too large to be part of any region and should always be studied as a completely independent geographic unit
hints: Locate Egypt using a map: does it touch the Mediterranean, and which side? Then consider why different sources might group it differently.
Think about Turkey as an example—does it belong to one region only, or can geographers justify placing it in more than one region?

problemText: A geography student needs to identify a region from a written description. The description says the region has no coastline on the Pacific Ocean or the Indian Ocean. Based on the five major Asian regions—Central Asia, South Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and Oceania—which region matches that description?
choices: South Asia
Central Asia
East Asia
Southeast Asia
hints: Only one of the five regions is landlocked with no ocean coastline at all.
This region sits in the interior of the continent, surrounded by land on all sides.

problemText: A map shows two regions: one touches only the Pacific Ocean and lies north of another region; the second region touches both the Pacific Ocean and the Indian Ocean. The five regions are Central Asia, South Asia, East Asia, Southeast Asia, and Oceania. Which is the southern region that touches both oceans?
choices: Oceania
South Asia
Southeast Asia
Central Asia
hints: The region that touches both named oceans lies between two other regions on the continent.
Think about which region sits east of South Asia and south of East Asia at the same time.

problemText: A student is reading about Oceania and finds two different definitions in two different geography sources. The first source says Oceania includes only the Pacific island groups, while the second source says Oceania includes the Pacific island groups and also a large continent. Which statement explains why these two sources give different definitions?
choices: Oceania's boundaries have changed over time, and the two sources are using definitions from different historical periods.
One source is wrong and the other is correct according to the official world geography rules that all geographers must follow.
The second source accidentally included a continent that belongs to Asia, making its definition too broad compared to the first source's narrower focus.
Different sources draw the boundaries of Oceania differently; the region's borders and definition are not settled the same way by every source.
hints: Geographic regions can be named and divided into sub-regions in different ways by different sources.
Just as continents are divided into sub-regions in multiple ways, a region like Oceania can be defined differently by different sources and still be acceptable.

problemText: A clue says: "This region lies directly south of Central Asia, and its southern edge forms a peninsula that reaches into the Indian Ocean." Using geography facts, first determine which ocean it touches. Then, determine which region sits north of it. Name the region.
choices: South Asia
Southeast Asia
East Asia
Oceania
hints: Question one: Does this region touch the Indian Ocean, the Pacific, both, or neither? The word 'peninsula' should help you answer.
Question two: The clue says the region lies 'directly south of Central Asia.' Which of the five major Asian regions has Central Asia as its northern neighbor?

problemText: Two incorrect statements appear below about the five major Asian regions and their ocean coastlines. Statement 1: "East Asia is the only region that touches the Pacific Ocean." Statement 2: "South Asia has no coastline on the Indian Ocean." Which pair of corrections states the true facts?
choices: East Asia is the only region touching the Pacific Ocean, which makes statement 1 correct. South Asia lies inland with no coastlines, which makes statement 2 correct.
East Asia touches the Pacific Ocean, but Southeast Asia and Oceania also touch the Pacific. South Asia does reach the Indian Ocean through its southern peninsula.
East Asia touches both the Pacific and Atlantic Oceans, so statement 1 is incorrect. South Asia touches only the Indian Ocean and not the Pacific, so statement 2 is partially correct.
East Asia lies along the Pacific coastline, and Southeast Asia also borders this ocean. South Asia is completely landlocked in the interior of Asia with no ocean access.
hints: For statement 1, remember that more than one region touches the Pacific Ocean. Name the regions that have a Pacific coastline.
For statement 2, think about the peninsula geography of South Asia. Does a peninsula formed in the Indian Ocean mean no coastline on that ocean?

problemText: A student reads this incorrect summary: "Central Asia and East Asia both lie on the mainland of the Asian continent and both touch the Indian Ocean, making them similar in location. Southeast Asia, by contrast, is very different because it is the only region that touches an ocean." Based on the geography of the five major Asian regions, how many separate location-related facts in this summary are wrong?
choices: Two errors: Central Asia and East Asia are the same because neither touches the Indian Ocean, and Southeast Asia is different because it touches both oceans.
One error: East Asia does not actually touch the Indian Ocean; it touches only the Pacific.
Three errors: Central Asia touches no ocean, East Asia touches only the Pacific (not the Indian), and Southeast Asia is not the only region that touches an ocean.
Four errors: Every statement in the summary contradicts what geography teaches about the locations and oceans of these regions.
hints: Go through the summary sentence by sentence. For Central Asia, does it touch the Indian Ocean? For East Asia, does it touch the Indian Ocean or only the Pacific? For Southeast Asia, is it the only region with an ocean?
Central Asia is landlocked, East Asia touches one ocean, and at least three regions touch the Pacific Ocean, while at least two touch the Indian Ocean.
